lmsArticle.title: Types of Locks Explained: Optimistic vs. Pessimistic Locking
lmsArticle.subtitle: How do you prevent two users from editing the same record at the same time? We compare Optimistic Locking (Versioning) and Pessimistic Locking (Databa
lmsArticle.excerpt: Pessimistic locking locks the record *before* editing — safe but slower under low contention. Optimistic locking checks for changes *before saving* using a version number — fast but can fail and require retry under high contention. Choosing correctly depends on your write-conflict probability.
lmsArticle.content:
## Scenario context

Pessimistic locking locks the record *before* editing — safe but slower under low contention. Optimistic locking checks for changes *before saving* using a version number — fast but can fail and require retry under high contention. Choosing correctly depends on your write-conflict probability.

---

Imagine a Shared Google Doc. Two people open it simultaneously and both start typing.

- **Pessimistic approach:** Onl…

This walkthrough focuses on **Two Ways to Prevent the Concurrent Edit Problem**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- Two people open it simultaneously and both start typing.
- - Pessimistic approach: Only one person can type at a time.
- The doc is "locked" for everyone else until the first person finishes.

**Concepts in play:** transaction-isolation-distributed-acid, caching, jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection, consistency-replication

## Stage 1 — Locking Fundamentals: Concurrency and Write Conflicts

- Before picking a locking strategy, it helps to understand exactly what can go wrong without one.
- When two transactions read and write the same row at overlapping times, the database can produce incorrect results — silently.
- These are called concurrency anomalies .
- Locking prevents these anomalies by serialising access to shared data.

*Applies **transaction-isolation-distributed-acid** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Locking prevents these anomalies by serialising access to shared data.

## Stage 2 — Pessimistic Locking: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE

- Pessimistic locking acquires an exclusive database lock on a row before any modification.
- While Transaction A holds the lock, Transaction B's SELECT ...
- FOR UPDATE on the same row blocks until A commits or rolls back.
- 📊 Lock State Machine Lock types: Deadlock risk: Transaction A holds Row 1, wants Row 2.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

```sql
-- Transaction A: lock the row
BEGIN TRANSACTION;
SELECT * FROM inventory WHERE product_id = 42 FOR UPDATE;

-- Now safely modify
UPDATE inventory SET quantity = quantity - 1 WHERE product_id = 42;
COMMIT TRANSACTION;
```

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Transaction A
    participant B as Transaction B
    participant DB as Database

    A->>DB: BEGIN + SELECT FOR UPDATE (product 42)
    DB-->>A: Row locked
    B->>DB: SELECT FOR UPDATE (product 42)
    DB-->>B: Waiting for lock...
    A->>DB: UPDATE + COMMIT
    DB-->>B: Lock acquired
    B->>DB: UPDATE + COMMIT
```

**Observable outcome:** 📊 Lock State Machine Lock types: Deadlock risk: Transaction A holds Row 1, wants Row 2.

## Stage 3 — Optimistic Locking: Version Column Pattern

- Optimistic locking adds a version column.
- No lock is held during the read — only at write time does the system check whether anyone else modified the row first.
- In Java with JPA: JPA throws OptimisticLockException when the version check fails — the calling service must catch it and retry.

*Applies **jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection** to the decision above.*

```sql
-- Step 1: Read with version
SELECT id, balance, version FROM accounts WHERE id = 1;
-- Returns: { id: 1, balance: 1000, version: 3 }

-- Step 2: Update with version check
UPDATE accounts
SET balance = 900, version = 4         -- increment version
WHERE id = 1 AND version = 3;          -- only if version unchanged

-- Step 3: Check affected rows
-- 1 row affected = success
-- 0 rows affected = conflict → retry
```

```java
@Entity
public class Account {
    @Id Long id;
    double balance;

    @Version          // JPA manages optimistic locking automatically
    int version;
}
```

**Observable outcome:** In Java with JPA: JPA throws OptimisticLockException when the version check fails — the calling service must catch it and retry.

## Stage 4 — Deep Dive: How Database Locks Are Implemented

- Databases implement pessimistic locks via a lock manager : an in-memory hash table keyed by (table, row) that tracks which transaction holds each lock and which are waiting.
- The lock manager periodically scans wait queues for cycles to detect deadlocks, then rolls back one transaction as the victim.
- Optimistic locking needs no lock manager — the version check happens inside the UPDATE statement itself, handled entirely by the storage engine at commit time.

*Applies **consistency-replication** to the decision above.*

```architecture
{
  "version": 1,
  "title": "Deep Dive: How Database Locks Are Implemented - Storage Topology",
  "description": "Multi-tier caching and replicated storage pipeline ensuring fast reads and transactional consistency.",
  "view": "data-flow",
  "pattern": "cache-aside",
  "direction": "LR",
  "groups": [
    { "id": "compute", "label": "Application Workers", "tone": "blue" },
    { "id": "cache-tier", "label": "Volatile Memory Tier", "tone": "amber" },
    { "id": "storage-tier", "label": "Persistent Disk Tier", "tone": "green" }
  ],
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "worker", "component": "workflow-service", "label": "Worker Process", "group": "compute" },
    { "id": "mem", "component": "redis", "label": "In-Memory Cache", "group": "cache-tier", "badge": "Hot Keys" },
    { "id": "primary", "component": "postgres", "label": "Primary Database", "group": "storage-tier", "badge": "Write Master" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "worker", "to": "mem", "kind": "read", "label": "Fast Read" },
    { "from": "worker", "to": "primary", "kind": "write", "label": "Transactional Commit" }
  ],
  "takeaway": {
    "title": "Storage Access Pattern",
    "body": "In-memory caching handles high-frequency read spikes, reserving disk transactions strictly for state modifications."
  }
}
```

**Observable outcome:** Optimistic locking needs no lock manager — the version check happens inside the UPDATE statement itself, handled entirely by the storage engine at commit time.

## Stage 5 — Choosing Your Lock Strategy

- The decision between pessimistic and optimistic locking is primarily a question of conflict frequency .
- Use the flowchart below as a quick decision guide, then validate against your observed write-conflict rate in production.
- 📊 Lock Type Selection Decision Tree If your write-conflict rate sits between 5 % and 10 %, measure under realistic load before deciding.
- Optimistic locking's retry overhead compounds quickly when conflicts are frequent, so a brief load test is worth the effort before committing to a strategy.

*Applies **transaction-isolation-distributed-acid** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Write operation needed] --> B{How frequent are write conflicts?}
    B -->|High - more than 10 percent| C[Use Pessimistic Locking]
    B -->|Low - less than 5 percent| D[Use Optimistic Locking]
    C --> E{Single row or multiple rows?}
    E -->|Single row| F[SELECT FOR UPDATE]
    E -->|Multiple rows| G[Lock in consistent order to prevent deadlock]
    D --> H[Add version column to table]
    H --> I{Conflict detected on save?}
    I -->|Yes| J[Throw OptimisticLockException - retry]
    I -->|No| K[Commit successfully]
```

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Choose a lock strategy] --> B{Concurrent reads frequent?}
    B -- Yes --> C{Writes also frequent?}
    C -- No --> D[ReadWriteLock shared reads / exclusive writes]
    C -- Yes --> E[Pessimistic row lock]
    B -- No --> F{Single-threaded access?}
    F -- Yes --> G[No lock needed]
    F -- No --> H{Low conflict probability?}
    H -- Yes --> I[Optimistic MVCC version column]
    H -- No --> J[Pessimistic lock SELECT FOR UPDATE]
```

**Observable outcome:** Optimistic locking's retry overhead compounds quickly when conflicts are frequent, so a brief load test is worth the effort before committing to a strategy.

## Stage 6 — Real-World Applications: Choosing the Right Strategy for Real Systems

## End-to-end outcome

After working through the stages, you should be able to explain:

- Choosing the wrong lock strategy leads to either lost updates (under-locking) or throughput bottlenecks (over-locking).
- Keep these four rules of thumb handy: 1.

seriesList.name: Architecture Patterns for Production Systems
seriesList.description: High-level design is only half the battle; the other half is surviving production. This series explores the architectural patterns required to build resilient, scalable, and maintainable systems. We dive into the trade-offs of microservices vs. monoliths, event-driven architectures, caching strategies, and data consistency models. Each post focuses on proven patterns that solve common bottlenecks in high-traffic production environments, helping you move from "it works on my machine" to "it works at scale."

seriesList.name: Low-Level Design Guide
seriesList.description: Good architecture is built on a foundation of solid low-level design. This series is a deep dive into the "micro" side of software engineering—focusing on class design, object-oriented principles (SOLID), and tactical design patterns. We explore how to translate requirements into clean, maintainable code, handle concurrency at the component level, and define clear interfaces. Whether you're preparing for LLD interviews or looking to sharpen your day-to-day coding craftsmanship, this guide provides the blueprints for building modular software.

seriesList.name: How It Works: Internals Explained
seriesList.description: Ever wondered what actually happens when you trigger a function, commit a transaction, or deploy a container? This series peels back the layers of abstraction to explore the low-level mechanics of modern technology. From database engines and operating system internals to the hidden plumbing of distributed systems, we dive deep into the source code and architectural designs that make complex software work. No magic, just engineering.

seriesList.name: Software Engineering Principles
seriesList.description: Writing code is easy; engineering software that lasts is hard. This series explores the core philosophies and mental models that define professional software development. We go beyond syntax to discuss the timeless principles of modularity, abstraction, testing strategies, and technical debt management. Whether we’re discussing the Zen of Python or the rigors of formal verification, this series provides a high-level perspective on how to think like an engineer, not just a coder.
